items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: Medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round
items.claim: The idea that 'medieval people thought the Earth was flat' was popularised in the 19th century. Who is most responsible for spreading it?

options.text: Galileo, in his trial defence of 1633
Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which fabricated a debate at Salamanca about whether Columbus would sail off the edge
Karl Marx, as part of his critique of religion

items.reveal:
Bede (8th century), Aquinas (13th century), Dante (14th century) and the entire scholastic tradition assumed a spherical Earth — it was Aristotelian orthodoxy reinforced by Ptolemy. Columbus's argument with the Salamanca scholars was about the Earth's circumference, not its shape; they thought (correctly) it was too large to sail to Asia westward.

Washington Irving's 'A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (1828) was a partly fictionalised popular biography. It invented the flat-Earth debate to make Columbus look more visionary. The myth then became a stock anti-medieval, anti-Catholic talking point in the late 19th century (notably John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White).
items.why: Historiography matters. The 'Dark Ages' frame and the flat-Earth myth are products of later polemic, not medieval thought. The conflict-between-science-and-religion narrative is largely a 19th-century construction.
